rv.q: This is a beautiful, heartbreaking response to Chekhov’s tragicomedy, which drills into its essence and marvels afresh at the playwright’s ability to craft characters that feel so recognisable.
It is a truly remarkable stage performance, that seems to go beyond acting and on to something like a shamanic act of empathy.
It’s a masterclass in actorly skill, in tone and pacing.

One Irish actor playing eight parts in an English-language spin on a Russian play that is 125 years old manages, magically, to offer as bleak and searing an exposé of the human condition as it is possible to get.
Scott’s performance has a raw intensity that ignites this ingenious staging.
This is not merely an acting showcase; it is a joint remoulding.
It is utterly mesmerising and thrillingly theatrical.
Much I have seen on stage, post-Covid, has lacked daring, so this emotionally charged piece of event theatre feels like an eccentrically welcome arrival in the West End.

Scott flits between characters, male and female, sounding off as the bitter Vanya, demurely twiddling a necklace as the lovely Helena. Meet, too, the handsome doctor, Michael, an eco-bore who drinks, and the sad, on-the-shelf Sonia. Emotions here are raw, crushes are unrequited and all hopes are dashed.
Those who come to see Scott on stage will not leave disappointed.
If you can handle that much radiance at once, then Vanya is remarkable, deluxe craftsmanship credited to four masterful creators.
The case is not made here that that is a job best assigned to only one person.
Genuine hilarity goes hand-in-hand with arresting depth, generating an exceptionally eclectic and relentlessly engaging piece of theatre.
It is so full of feeling and empathy that you cannot quite believe that you are actually watching a single man sitting alone, holding the arm of a chair. It is a great achievement.
You won't find a more remarkable actor doing a more remarkable piece of theatre anywhere in the West End.
Powerful and brave, Vanya is a meditation on existence itself.
He makes a decent fist of Alexander, the crotchety professor with a disabling limp.
If you want to see Chekhov’s play, there no sense in going to the Duke of York’s Theatre.
Scott is a dextrous and enthralling actor but even he cannot replicate the subtle agony of Chekhov's characters on his own.

cn.t: Andrew Scott delivers a tour-de-force performance in this one-man adaptation of Chekhov's classic, though critics split on whether it transcends its high-concept gimmick. Most praise his remarkable versatility, but some find it overindulgent.
